pos: n. pl. (the priestly house of Aaron, reckoned as a company; named twice)
etymology: Patronymic plural from Aaron; the Authorized Version's rendering for the house of Aaron considered as a body of men, 1 Chronicles 12:27 and 27:17.
biblical_def: The Aaronites are the priestly family counted as a company among the forces that came to David: “And Jehoiada was the leader of the Aaronites, and with him were three thousand and seven hundred” (1 Chronicles 12:27). The next verse names the man who would matter most: “And Zadok, a young man mighty of valour, and of his father's house twenty and two captains” (1 Chronicles 12:28). Zadok appears again at the head of the house in the administrative lists of David's reign: “Of the Levites, Hashabiah the son of Kemuel: of the Aaronites, Zadok” (1 Chronicles 27:17). The sons of Aaron were not a tribe but a family within Levi, and theirs alone was the altar: “Therefore thou and thy sons with thee shall keep your priest's office for every thing of the altar, and within the vail; and ye shall serve: I have given your priest's office unto you as a service of gift: and the stranger that cometh nigh shall be put to death” (Numbers 18:7). Three thousand seven hundred Aaronites came to David's side, which is to say that the priesthood as a body declared for the man God had anointed. The priest's office is called a service of gift, not a right seized, and that is the whole doctrine of the name.

corruption_summary: The Aaronic priesthood is made the pattern for a sacrificing clergy in the church, where the New Testament ends that priesthood in Christ and gives no altar to men.
corruption_paragraphs: Rome reasons from Aaron to the Mass: if God once appointed a sacrificing priesthood with an altar and a set-apart caste, the church must have the same. The epistle to the Hebrews answers the argument directly. The Aaronic priesthood was by the law, was many because its priests died, and offered sacrifices that could never take away sins; Christ's priesthood is by an oath, is unchangeable because He ever liveth, and rests on one offering made once. To re-erect an order of men who offer is to deny that the one offering was finished.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the phrase Numbers uses: the priest's office is a service of gift. No man took that honour to himself, and the stranger who came near was to die. The church has two offices, elder and deacon, and one Priest, and her ministers serve a table and not an altar.

pos: n. pl. (the tribe of Asher, named in the indictment of Judges 1; named once)
etymology: Patronymic plural from Asher, Hebrew 'Asher, happy or blessed; used once, Judges 1:32.
biblical_def: The Asherites are named once, and the verse is an indictment: “But the Asherites dwelt among the Canaanites, the inhabitants of the land: for they did not drive them out” (Judges 1:32). The sentence before it lists the towns they failed to take: “Neither did Asher drive out the inhabitants of Accho, nor the inhabitants of Zidon, nor of Ahlab, nor of Achzib, nor of Helbah, nor of Aphik, nor of Rehob” (Judges 1:31). The order of the words in verse 32 is the whole point. It does not say the Canaanites dwelt among the Asherites, as though Israel had tolerated a remnant in its own land; it says the Asherites dwelt among the Canaanites, which is the posture of a minority settling in. The charge had been explicit: “And ye shall make no league with the inhabitants of this land; ye shall throw down their altars: but ye have not obeyed my voice: why have ye done this?” (Judges 2:2). The sentence followed the disobedience: “Wherefore I also said, I will not drive them out from before you; but they shall be as thorns in your sides, and their gods shall be a snare unto you” (Judges 2:3). The whole book of Judges is the working out of that verse, and Asher's name means happy.

corruption_summary: Israel's failure to separate is praised as early pluralism, where Judges treats it as disobedience and names the consequence.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern treatments of Judges 1 frequently commend what the chapter condemns: the tribes that left the Canaanites in place are presented as practising a wise coexistence, and the command to drive them out as the harsher, later theology. The text gives the verdict itself, in God's own words: ye have not obeyed my voice, and the gods of these peoples shall be a snare unto you (Judges 2:2-3). The rest of the book proves it true, cycle after cycle, with Israel serving Baalim and crying out and being delivered and turning back again.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that compromise is never static. Asher did not drive them out, and so Asher dwelt among them; a tribe that will not deal with what God commanded it to remove ends up living on its terms. Separation in Scripture is never hatred of men but refusal of their altars.

pos: n. pl. (the people of Ashdod, one of the five Philistine lordships; named once)
etymology: Gentilic plural from Ashdod, Hebrew 'Ashdod, a stronghold; one of the five cities of the Philistine confederacy, Joshua 13:3.
biblical_def: The Ashdothites are named once, in the survey of land still unconquered: “From Sihor, which is before Egypt, even unto the borders of Ekron northward, which is counted to the Canaanite: five lords of the Philistines; the Gazathites, and the Ashdothites, the Eshkalonites, the Gittites, and the Ekronites; also the Avites” (Joshua 13:3). The occasion of the list is given in the verse before: “Now Joshua was old and stricken in years; and the LORD said unto him, Thou art old and stricken in years, and there remaineth yet very much land to be possessed” (Joshua 13:1). Ashdod is the city to which the ark was first carried after Israel's defeat at Ebenezer: “And the Philistines took the ark of God, and brought it from Ebenezer unto Ashdod” (1 Samuel 5:1). What happened there is the most eloquent thing Scripture records of the place: “And when they arose early on the morrow morning, behold, Dagon was fallen upon his face to the ground before the ark of the LORD; and the head of Dagon and both the palms of his hands were cut off upon the threshold; only the stump of Dagon was left to him” (1 Samuel 5:4). Israel had lost a battle and the ark was in a heathen temple, and the idol lay broken before it with no Israelite in the room.

corruption_summary: The fall of Dagon is read as folklore, where 1 Samuel 5 reports it as the LORD vindicating His own name when His people could not.
corruption_paragraphs: The account of Dagon broken on his threshold is treated as legend of the kind temples tell about rival gods. The narrative's own shape argues otherwise. Israel had just been beaten in the field, the priesthood had been killed, and the ark was taken; by every visible measure Dagon had won, and the Philistines set the ark in his house as a trophy. What follows is a defeat no Israelite witnessed, arranged, or could report as propaganda — and the chapter continues with plagues on the cities until the Philistines themselves sent the ark home with an offering.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God is not dependent on His people's success for His glory. He let the ark go into captivity and then defended His honour alone, in a shut temple, before a stone idol. The chapter is a standing answer to the fear that God's cause fails when His servants do.

pos: n. pl. (an early people of the coast, and a resettled people in Samaria; named twice)
etymology: Gentilic plural; at Joshua 13:3 an old people of the Philistine coast, and at 2 Kings 17:31 one of the nations planted in Samaria by Assyria.
biblical_def: The Avites are named twice, and the two notices stand far apart. The first adds them to the unconquered peoples of the coast: “five lords of the Philistines; the Gazathites, and the Ashdothites, the Eshkalonites, the Gittites, and the Ekronites; also the Avites” (Joshua 13:3). The second places a people of that name among the colonists Assyria settled in the emptied land of Israel, and records what they brought with them: “And the Avites made Nibhaz and Tartak, and the Sepharvites burnt their children in fire to Adrammelech and Anammelech, the gods of Sepharvaim” (2 Kings 17:31). That chapter is the most careful account in Scripture of how a false religion is assembled: “Howbeit every nation made gods of their own, and put them in the houses of the high places which the Samaritans had made, every nation in their cities wherein they dwelt” (2 Kings 17:29). And it names the result in one sentence that has never gone out of date: “They feared the LORD, and served their own gods, after the manner of the nations whom they carried away from thence” (2 Kings 17:33). The Avites contributed two idols to that mixture, and the mixture is what the Samaritans of the Gospels inherited.

corruption_summary: Mixed religion is commended as tolerant breadth, where 2 Kings 17 records it as the thing that emptied the land and names it a lie.
corruption_paragraphs: The religion described in 2 Kings 17 is exactly what our age asks for: every nation keeping its own gods, all the shrines housed together, and the LORD acknowledged alongside the rest. Scripture's judgment on the arrangement is in a single verse — “They feared the LORD, and served their own gods” (2 Kings 17:33) — and the chapter has already explained that the land was emptied of Israel for the same sin in a native form. A God who will share His worship is not the God of Scripture, and the first commandment is not a preference.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that syncretism is not a half-way house toward faith but a settled substitute for it. The Avites brought Nibhaz and Tartak into the land where the ark had been, and their descendants were still disputing about the right mountain for worship when the Lord met a woman at a well there.

pos: n. pl. (the people of Ekron, northernmost of the Philistine lordships; named twice)
etymology: Gentilic plural from Ekron, Hebrew 'Eqron, probably from a root meaning to uproot; the northernmost of the five Philistine cities, Joshua 13:3.
biblical_def: The Ekronites are named in the survey of the land yet to be taken: “From Sihor, which is before Egypt, even unto the borders of Ekron northward, which is counted to the Canaanite: five lords of the Philistines; the Gazathites, and the Ashdothites, the Eshkalonites, the Gittites, and the Ekronites; also the Avites” (Joshua 13:3), the list being occasioned by the LORD's word to an old man: “Thou art old and stricken in years, and there remaineth yet very much land to be possessed” (Joshua 13:1). Ekron is also the last stop of the captured ark, and the Ekronites wanted nothing to do with it; the plague that had followed the ark from Ashdod to Gath came to them, and their lords met in council: “So they sent and gathered together all the lords of the Philistines, and said, Send away the ark of the God of Israel, and let it go again to his own place, that it slay us not, and our people: for there was a deadly destruction throughout all the city; the hand of God was very heavy there” (1 Samuel 5:11). The ark went home on a cart drawn by two cows, with a trespass offering of gold, and the Philistine rulers followed it to the border and watched: “And when the five lords of the Philistines had seen it, they returned to Ekron the same day” (1 Samuel 6:16).

corruption_summary: The plagues on the Philistine cities are explained as coincidence or epidemic, where the Philistines themselves drew the conclusion and acted on it.
corruption_paragraphs: The sickness that moved city by city with the ark is readily explained away as an epidemic following a captured object, and modern treatments are content to leave it there. The narrative's witnesses were not. The men who concluded that the hand of the God of Israel was heavy upon them were the Philistines, who had every reason to want another explanation; they consulted their own priests and diviners, devised a test with untrained milch cows that would have gone home to their calves, and watched the cart take the ark straight to Israel.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the enemies of God sometimes reason better about His acts than His own people do. Israel had taken the ark into battle as a charm and lost it; the Ekronites, who had no covenant, worked out that they were dealing with a living God and sent Him away with an offering.

pos: n. pl. (the people of Elam, east of Babylonia; named twice)
etymology: Gentilic plural from Elam, a son of Shem (Genesis 10:22) and the region east of Babylonia that bore his name; Ezra 4:9 and Acts 2:9.
biblical_def: The Elamites are named twice, and the two occurrences stand at opposite ends of the story. The first has them among the peoples who wrote to the Persian court against the rebuilding of Jerusalem: “Then wrote Rehum the chancellor, and Shimshai the scribe, and the rest of their companions; the Dinaites, the Apharsathchites, the Tarpelites, the Apharsites, the Archevites, the Babylonians, the Susanchites, the Dehavites, and the Elamites” (Ezra 4:9). The second has them in Jerusalem at Pentecost, hearing the gospel: “Parthians, and Medes, and Elamites, and the dwellers in Mesopotamia, and in Judaea, and Cappadocia, in Pontus, and Asia” (Acts 2:9), and what they heard is stated plainly: “Cretes and Arabians, we do hear them speak in our tongues the wonderful works of God” (Acts 2:11). The nation descends from Shem: “The children of Shem; Elam, and Asshur, and Arphaxad, and Lud, and Aram” (Genesis 10:22). A people who had signed a letter to stop the building of the temple were, five centuries later, among the first to hear in their own tongue that the true temple had been raised in three days.

corruption_summary: Pentecost is reduced to an ecstatic episode or to a symbol of diversity, where Acts 2 describes understood languages and a preached message.
corruption_paragraphs: Two readings of Pentecost are common and both miss the text. The first makes the tongues unintelligible ecstatic utterance; but the hearers say they heard “in our tongues the wonderful works of God” (Acts 2:11), and the list of nations exists to prove the languages were real. The second makes the day a celebration of diversity as such; but the chapter is a sermon from Joel and the Psalms ending in a call to repent and be baptized, and three thousand were added. The miracle served the preaching; it did not replace it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the reversal of Babel. At Babel one language was divided and men were scattered; at Pentecost many languages were given one message and men were gathered. The Elamites who once wrote to stop a building heard, in their own speech, of the One who is the foundation.

pos: n. pl. (the Levitical family of Amram, father of Moses and Aaron; named twice)
etymology: Patronymic plural from Amram, Hebrew 'Amram, exalted people or kindred of the high one; one of the four Kohathite families, Numbers 3:27.
biblical_def: The Amramites are the first-named of the four families of Kohath: “And of Kohath was the family of the Amramites, and the family of the Izeharites, and the family of the Hebronites, and the family of the Uzzielites: these are the families of the Kohathites” (Numbers 3:27). The same four stand together in David's register of the Levites: “Of the Amramites, and the Izharites, the Hebronites, and the Uzzielites” (1 Chronicles 26:23). Amram himself is the father of the two men who led Israel out of Egypt: “And Amram took him Jochebed his father's sister to wife; and she bare him Aaron and Moses: and the years of the life of Amram were an hundred and thirty and seven years” (Exodus 6:20). The Kohathites were given the holiest charge of the tabernacle's furniture: “And their charge shall be the ark, and the table, and the candlestick, and the altars, and the vessels of the sanctuary wherewith they minister, and the hanging, and all the service thereof” (Numbers 3:31). So the family of Amram carried the ark on its shoulders and gave Israel its lawgiver and its first high priest, and Scripture records the whole of it in the flat voice of a register, as one family among four.

corruption_summary: Moses is treated as a legendary founder without a family, where Scripture gives his parents, his tribe, his clan and his exact Levitical house.
corruption_paragraphs: A standard critical position holds that Moses is a legendary figure around whom a nation's founding traditions gathered. The registers make an inconvenient witness. Scripture places him in a named family within a named clan within a named tribe, gives his father's name and his mother's, states their relation to one another, records his father's age at death, names his brother and his sister, and lists his descendants. Founding legends are not usually furnished with clan genealogies that also record the family's later duties in moving furniture.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the ordinariness of the means God uses. The Amramites are the first of four Kohathite families in a census, and out of that household came the man who spoke with God face to face. Scripture puts the lawgiver in a register, because the covenant runs through households.

pos: n. pl. (used of the heights of Hermon in Psalm 42; named once)
etymology: Gentilic plural from Hermon, Hebrew Chermon, from charam, to devote or set apart; the Authorized Version's rendering of the Hebrew plural for the peaks or region of Hermon, Psalm 42:6.
biblical_def: Hermonites occurs once, in the psalm of a man exiled from the sanctuary: “O my God, my soul is cast down within me: therefore will I remember thee from the land of Jordan, and of the Hermonites, from the hill Mizar” (Psalm 42:6). The Hebrew is a plural, and the Authorized Version renders it as a people-name; the sense is the heights of Hermon and the country about them, far to the north of Jerusalem, where Jordan rises. The geography is the grief. The psalmist is at the headwaters, among foreign hills, remembering the house of God he cannot reach, and the whole psalm is built on that distance: “To the chief Musician, Maschil, for the sons of Korah. As the hart panteth after the water brooks, so panteth my soul after thee, O God” (Psalm 42:1). Twice he preaches to himself rather than listening to himself: “Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted in me? hope thou in God: for I shall yet praise him for the help of his countenance” (Psalm 42:5). The one place in Scripture where the word stands is therefore a place of exile and of resolved hope, and the resolution is a command a believer gives his own soul.

corruption_summary: The psalmist's distress is treated as a clinical condition to be managed, where he addresses his own soul with the command to hope in God.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 42 is the text most often enlisted to baptize the therapeutic account of the inner life: the sufferer is validated, his feelings are honoured, and the psalm is read as permission to sit in them. The psalm does honour the grief — it says the soul is cast down and does not pretend otherwise — and then it does what no therapy does. It issues a command: hope thou in God. The man speaks to himself in the imperative, on the ground of a promise, and he grounds his comfort in the help of God's countenance rather than in the resolution of his circumstances.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that affliction is real and is not sovereign. From the land of Jordan and of the Hermonites, cut off from the courts he loved, the psalmist remembered God on purpose, and the remembering was an act and not a mood.

pos: n. (a people descended from Canaan, named in the table of nations; named twice)
etymology: Gentilic from Hamath, Hebrew Chamath, a fortress or enclosure; the last-named of the families of Canaan, Genesis 10:18 and 1 Chronicles 1:16.
biblical_def: The Hamathite closes the list of Canaan's families in the table of nations: “And the Arvadite, and the Zemarite, and the Hamathite: and afterward were the families of the Canaanites spread abroad” (Genesis 10:18), and Chronicles repeats the three in the same order: “And the Arvadite, and the Zemarite, and the Hamathite” (1 Chronicles 1:16). The head of the line is given a few verses earlier: “And Canaan begat Sidon his firstborn, and Heth” (Genesis 10:15). Hamath itself was a great city on the Orontes to the north, and the phrase the entering in of Hamath marks Israel's northern boundary again and again in Scripture. Amos used it in a rebuke to those at ease in Zion, pointing them to cities that had fallen: “Pass ye unto Calneh, and see; and from thence go ye to Hamath the great: then go down to Gath of the Philistines: be they better than these kingdoms? or their border greater than your border?” (Amos 6:2). The table of nations is the Bible's account of one human family divided into peoples, and the Hamathite is a line in it.

corruption_summary: The table of nations is read as a charter for racial hierarchy, where Genesis 10 traces every nation to one family and grounds the unity of mankind.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 10 has been abused in two directions. It has been used, shamefully, to justify racial subjugation, chiefly by misreading the curse on Canaan as a curse on a skin colour, which the text nowhere says and which the list itself refutes by making Canaan one family among the Hamites of the Levant. And it is now used in the reverse direction, as evidence that Scripture is itself an ethnic-hierarchy document to be set aside. Both readings require the chapter to say what it does not. It traces every nation on earth to three brothers in one household.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one Paul preached at Athens: God hath made of one blood all nations of men. The biblical categories are one-in-Adam and one-in-Christ, and a table that puts the Hamathite, the Arvadite and the Zemarite in the same genealogy as every reader of it is the foundation of that doctrine, not an exception to it.

pos: n. (the designation of Ahithophel, David's counsellor, of Giloh; named twice)
etymology: Gentilic from Giloh, a town in the hill country of Judah; Hebrew Giloni, used of Ahithophel at 2 Samuel 15:12 and of his son Eliam at 23:34.
biblical_def: Gilonite is the designation of the most gifted traitor in Scripture: “And Absalom sent for Ahithophel the Gilonite, David's counsellor, from his city, even from Giloh, while he offered sacrifices. And the conspiracy was strong; for the people increased continually with Absalom” (2 Samuel 15:12). The word appears again of his son among David's thirty: “Eliphelet the son of Ahasbai, the son of the Maachathite, Eliam the son of Ahithophel the Gilonite” (2 Samuel 23:34). The measure of what David lost is given plainly: “And the counsel of Ahithophel, which he counselled in those days, was as if a man had enquired at the oracle of God: so was all the counsel of Ahithophel both with David and with Absalom” (2 Samuel 16:23). David's one prayer in the flight was that this counsel would be turned to foolishness, and it was; and the end of the man is one of the bleakest verses in the books of Samuel: “And when Ahithophel saw that his counsel was not followed, he saddled his ass, and arose, and gat him home to his house, to his city, and put his household in order, and hanged himself, and died, and was buried in the sepulchre of his father” (2 Samuel 17:23). A man of Giloh gave Israel its wisest advice and its clearest picture of a friend turned enemy.

corruption_summary: Ahithophel is excused as a man with grievances, where Scripture treats him as the pattern of the familiar friend who lifts up his heel.
corruption_paragraphs: Sympathetic treatments of Ahithophel supply him with motives: his son stood in David's guard, his granddaughter may have been Bathsheba, and a man so wronged may be forgiven for changing sides. Scripture does not take that road. It calls him David's counsellor and then shows him advising a son to destroy his father, and it treats his defection as the type of a betrayal still to come. The psalm that names him sets the pattern: the familiar friend, who ate bread with the king, lifting up his heel against him — words the Lord Jesus applied to Judas.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that natural gifts are no guarantee of a right heart. Counsel that was as the oracle of God came from a man who hanged himself in his own city; and the king who was betrayed, driven out barefoot over Kidron and weeping, is in that hour the plainest Old Testament picture of Christ.
